```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE
)
```

This package now tracks benchmark results in a regime-aware format rather than a
single pooled leaderboard. That matters because the right method depends on the
problem structure:

- are rows matched exactly or only weakly supervised?
- is overlap full or partial?
- are labels clean, noisy, or absent?
- do all domains share the same feature dimension?

This article reads the tracked synthetic benchmark outputs and turns them into
practical method guidance. The bundled tables are frozen historical outputs;
current `alignment_method_registry()` lifecycle states take precedence over
historical rankings.

## Load benchmark outputs

```{r read-results}
bench_dir <- system.file("extdata", "benchmark-guidance", package = "manifoldalign",
                         mustWork = TRUE)

rank_path <- file.path(bench_dir, "toy_feature_aligners_regime_ranks.csv")
seed_path <- file.path(bench_dir, "toy_feature_seed_audit_summary.csv")

stopifnot(file.exists(rank_path), file.exists(seed_path))

regime_ranks <- utils::read.csv(rank_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
seed_audit <- utils::read.csv(seed_path, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
full_registry <- manifoldalign:::synthetic_alignment_scenarios(profile = "full")

required_rank_cols <- c(
  "scenario", "supervision_regime", "dimensionality_constraint",
  "method", "method_family", "overall_rank",
  "runtime_sec_mean", "max_abs_latent_cor_mean", "centroid_acc_mean"
)
required_seed_cols <- c(
  "scenario", "method", "method_family", "supervision_regime",
  "centroid_acc_mean", "centroid_acc_cv", "max_abs_latent_cor_mean"
)

stopifnot(all(required_rank_cols %in% names(regime_ranks)))
stopifnot(all(required_seed_cols %in% names(seed_audit)))
stopifnot(nrow(regime_ranks) > 0, nrow(seed_audit) > 0)
```

## Coverage

The checked-in fast benchmark and the checked-in seed-audit summary do not have
to cover exactly the same scenario set. The fast benchmark is where we broaden
regime coverage; the seed audit is where we focus on stability diagnostics.

```{r coverage}
rank_scenarios <- sort(unique(regime_ranks$scenario))
seed_scenarios <- sort(unique(seed_audit$scenario))
full_scenarios <- sort(unique(full_registry$scenario))
full_only_scenarios <- setdiff(full_scenarios, rank_scenarios)

coverage <- data.frame(
  source = c(
    rep("fast_benchmark", length(rank_scenarios)),
    rep("seed_audit", length(seed_scenarios)),
    rep("full_registry_only", length(full_only_scenarios))
  ),
  scenario = c(rank_scenarios, seed_scenarios, full_only_scenarios),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

stopifnot(all(seed_scenarios %in% rank_scenarios | seed_scenarios %in% full_scenarios))
coverage
```

At the moment the checked-in fast benchmark covers the five lightweight feature
regimes:

- `linear_affine`
- `isometric_curve`
- `hard_nonisometric`
- `partial_open_set`
- `noisy_label_shift`

The full registry also defines `many_domain_consensus` and `highdim_stress`,
but those are kept in the `full` profile because they behave more like stress
tests than routine dev-loop benchmarks.

## Regime leaders

For each scenario and supervision regime we keep the top-ranked method after
combining runtime, latent correlation, and centroid recovery.

```{r regime-leaders}
leader_rows <- !duplicated(regime_ranks[c(
  "scenario", "supervision_regime", "dimensionality_constraint"
)])

leaders <- regime_ranks[leader_rows, c(
  "scenario", "supervision_regime", "dimensionality_constraint",
  "method", "method_family", "overall_rank",
  "runtime_sec_mean", "max_abs_latent_cor_mean", "centroid_acc_mean"
)]

leaders
```

Two patterns are immediate:

- `global_geo_rowid_exact` is now the strongest unrestricted
  exact-correspondence method on the full-overlap scenarios in the checked-in
  fast benchmark: `linear_affine`, `isometric_curve`, `hard_nonisometric`, and
  `noisy_label_shift`.
- `spectral_mnn_exact` still matters because it is the current leader on the
  partial/open-set exact-correspondence regime.
- In label-supervised regimes there is still no single winner:
  `kema_linear_label` leads on `linear_affine` and `isometric_curve`,
  `lowrank_label` leads on `hard_nonisometric`, and `gpca_label` leads on
  `noisy_label_shift`.
- The new multiset regimes are intentionally separate from the exact and label
  tables: `mma_consensus_unsupervised` leads the unsupervised-multiset blocks,
  and `multiset_uot_side_geometry` leads the transport-side-geometry blocks.

## Stability matters

Mean score alone is not enough. The seed audit tracks how much a method moves
across repeated random draws.

```{r variability}
seed_audit <- seed_audit[order(
  -seed_audit$centroid_acc_cv,
  -seed_audit$max_abs_latent_cor_mean,
  seed_audit$method
), ]

most_variable <- seed_audit[seq_len(min(10L, nrow(seed_audit))), c(
  "scenario", "method", "method_family", "supervision_regime",
  "centroid_acc_mean", "centroid_acc_cv",
  "max_abs_latent_cor_mean"
)]

stopifnot(all(is.finite(most_variable$centroid_acc_cv)))
most_variable
```

These tracked runs show:

- `gpca_label` is the safest label-supervised baseline in the audited core
  trio.
- `kema_linear_label` is fast and often strong on latent correlation, but its
  centroid recovery is materially more seed-sensitive on the nonlinear curve
  case.
- The multiscale family is still clearly more variable than the best exact and
  label-supervised baselines.
- The checked-in seed audit is intentionally narrower than the fast benchmark,
  so it should be read as a stability diagnostic for the core trio rather than
  as a full coverage table for every benchmarked regime.

## Practical guidance

The current toy benchmark supports these rules of thumb:

- Start with `global_geo_rowid_exact` when exact row correspondences are
  available and the problem has full overlap with shared global geometry.
- Reach for `spectral_mnn_exact` earlier when overlap is partial/open-set,
  because that is where it overtakes the other exact-correspondence methods in
  the checked-in fast benchmark.
- Use `gpca_label` as the safest label-supervised baseline and
  `lowrank_label` as the strongest current label baseline on the harder
  nonlinear regime.
- Use `kema_linear_label` when you care about latent geometry and speed, but
  validate it with repeated seeds or resamples rather than trusting a single
  run.
- Treat `mma_consensus_unsupervised` as the current multiset baseline when you
  want a 3+ domain method without explicit side information.
- Treat `multiset_uot_side_geometry` as a different regime entirely: it is the
  right comparison point when a shared geometry/template is part of the problem
  specification.
- Treat generalized Procrustes as a useful exact-ID baseline only when feature
  dimensions match across domains.
- Treat coupled diagonalization and the multiscale methods as active research
  families rather than the current default recommendation on these synthetic
  tasks.
- Use `cone_align` as the unsupervised pairwise baseline when no
  correspondences are available between two domains. It leads the
  `unsupervised_pairwise` regime on most scenarios via iterative Procrustes
  on spectral embeddings.
- Use `grasp` when the unsupervised pairwise problem involves hard nonlinear
  distortion, where its diffusion descriptors provide an advantage.
- Use `parrot` when you have partial anchor correspondences (a subset of
  matched rows). It is the only method currently benchmarked in the
  `partial_anchor` regime.
- See `vignette(“method-selection-guide”)` for the full decision flowchart
  across all method families.

## What to benchmark next

The benchmark registry now separates lightweight fast scenarios from heavier
stress scenarios. The next high-value comparisons are:

- check in full-profile summaries for `many_domain_consensus` and
  `highdim_stress`,
- add truly adversarial side-information settings rather than only noisy labels,
- integrate `fpgw` and `token_ot_graph_align` into the benchmark (both return
  `multiblock_biprojector` objects but need input format adapters),
- add `gromov_wasserstein` with a transport-plan quality metric or barycentric
  projection step,
- track runtime and failure rates explicitly as first-class outputs.

Those settings are exactly where pooled “best method” tables tend to be wrong.
Use regime-specific summaries instead.
